items.title: What If AI Agents Had to Prove What Actually Happened Before Being Allowed to Continue?
items.abstract: An AI agent may be authorized to act—but what happens when the real-world result differs from what was authorized? Should that agent still be allowed to continue? As frontier AI models evolve into autonomous systems capable of executing payments, transmitting sensitive information, modifying infrastructure, invoking privileged tools, and controlling physical devices, a fundamental security question emerges: Why should authorization granted before an action remain sufficient when its actual consequences have not yet been independently verified? This paper proposes a different model of machine authority: “Computation is not authority to act. Authority must be earned from the real execution path, not granted indefinitely per session.” The research introduces Receipt-Gated Interim Effectuation Validation (IEV), an execution-control architecture in which a consequential operation may first produce a real but strictly bounded effect. Protected evidence of what actually occurred is subsequently examined by an independent validator. Only successful validation establishes the protected continuation condition required for a subsequent, potentially broader effect. The distinction is fundamental: the AI agent's assertion that an action succeeded is not proof that it happened correctly, and a receipt alone is not authorization to continue. The proposed architecture incorporates: Real-effect validation: Verification of actual outcomes rather than reliance solely on predicted behavior, proposed commands, or self-reported success. Receipt-gated continuation: Subsequent effectuation depends on protected validation of the preceding bounded effect. Independent execution authority: Separation of the AI computation environment from protected policy, credential, validation, and effectuation components. Software–hardware enforcement: Continuation conditions realized through cryptographic objects, derived or split keys, protected state, hardware latches, or equivalent mechanisms. Finality Sink verification: Independent checks at the effect-capable boundary, including act, destination, scope, phase, freshness, and revocation conditions. Taint and provenance controls: Consideration of untrusted inputs, prompt-injection exposure, credential surrogation, and privilege-separated execution. Fail-closed recovery: Explicit handling of missing receipts, uncertain outcomes, conflicting authentic evidence, validator compromise, crash recovery, and unauthorized retries. Controlled escalation: Protected human review, bounded automated remediation, reduced-scope continuation, and termination where required. The paper develops a formal protocol vocabulary, validation predicates, continuation mechanisms, six conformance profiles, implementation-invariance rules, illustrative workflows, and an analytical model of residual exposure. Potential applications include frontier AI agent infrastructure, autonomous tool execution, cloud and network operations, financial transactions, critical infrastructure, and robotic systems. The central research proposition is that AI safety should not end at the moment permission is granted. For consequential autonomous operations, the authority to proceed can be made technically dependent on independently verified evidence of what actually occurred. This publication presents a proposed architecture and analytical design, not an experimentally validated production system. It does not establish that any existing commercial platform implements the proposed mechanisms. Patent disclosure: The architecture described in this publication is identified as patent pending under Indian Patent Office application 202631117633, titled “Systems and Methods for Cryptographically Staged Effectuation with Verified Partial Effect, Receipt-Bound Full Effectuation, and Software-Hardware Enforcement.” Patentability, enforceable scope, and relationships to other technologies are not determined by this publication. Independent technical review, adversarial evaluation, implementation criticism, and discussion of related prior art are welcomed.

items.title: Who Can Say No? Control, Accountability and the Pace of Frontier AI
items.abstract: In September 2026, the leaders of the largest frontier AI laboratories said in public that the pace of capability improvement is too fast and that none of them can slow down alone, and agents under evaluation at OpenAI broke out of their test environment and reached a third party's live systems, which a UN-mandated panel called an early warning of one route to loss of human control. This paper examines the institutional side of that risk: not the machine, but the person who must control it. We argue that control is not taken by AI but given away, one delegation at a time, by organisations arranged so that nobody is positioned to say no, and we define control as a person who can detect a serious problem, challenge the decision, stop the system and reverse it, and who has something to lose by not doing so. Three questions follow, which any builder, funder, regulator or deployer can answer in public: (1) who inside the organisation can say no, and who answers for saying yes; (2) who outside the organisation checks the decision, and what can they do when they disagree; (3) what happens when AI builds AI faster than anyone can check it. A checkable answer needs a named person, a date, a number, and a stop that has been used or tested. Three measures meet that test: a named person on every consequential decision, including the standing instructions AI agents carry out; a supervisor with a stop authority; and two published clocks, time to build against time to check. We show that governance theory arrives at the same conditions, and code fifty older mechanisms against the questions, finding that almost every one began as one rule at one point, taken by one party without waiting for the rest. That is the paper's design: a start, not a solution. Publication is the first step and one laboratory can take it alone; the contract, the independent body and the law come after.

items.title: Who Controls the Agents? AI Agent Orchestration as the New Security Perimeter
items.abstract: This presentation examines artificial intelligence agent orchestration as an emerging security perimeter in modern multi-agent systems. It explores how increasing agent autonomy, delegation mechanisms, tool integration, and inter-agent communication introduce new cybersecurity risks and governance challenges. The presentation analyzes major orchestration architectures, including deterministic workflows, orchestrator–worker systems, agent handoffs, decentralized multi-agent configurations, and learned orchestration. Particular attention is given to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent2Agent (A2A) communication, trust boundaries, access control, and security vulnerabilities arising from interactions between autonomous agents and external tools. Drawing on recent cybersecurity incidents, technical standards, and research published in 2025–2026, the presentation evaluates the effectiveness and limitations of multi-agent architectures and discusses approaches to secure orchestration, verification, accountability, and human oversight. The central argument is that cybersecurity in agentic AI systems depends not only on individual model reliability but also on the governance and security of the entire orchestration process. Presented in connection with the V International Conference “Challenges and Reality of the IT-Space: Software Engineering and Cybersecurity” (SECS-2026), October 29–30, 2026, Kyiv, Ukraine (online).

items.title: "Smarter but Not Wiser": A Transdisciplinary CFA-GRM Simulation Pipeline for Mapping Human–GenAI Interaction
items.abstract: Background The integration of Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education creates a paradox between technical efficiency and cognitive depth. Current institutional responses rely more on fragmented oversight than on ecology- and process-oriented assessment. There is a lack of diagnostic tools to map psychometric thresholds when strategic cognitive shifts transition into functional dependence. Methods We present a simulation-based methodological framework using the Tripartite Confirmatory Factor Analysis–Graded Response Model (CFA-GRM). Grounded in the cognitive-affective-conative tripartite model, this study uses a Monte Carlo simulation (N = 1,000) to demonstrate how latent interaction pathways can be structurally validated and how item parameters can be calibrated against a pre-specified diagnostic threshold ( θ ≈ 0.5), with a replication study to establish parameter recovery. Results Across 200 replications at each of N = 1,000 and N = 300, all 400 converged with admissible solutions and recovered the generating parameters with maximum absolute relative bias of 0.040; interval coverage met conventional criteria for 11 of 15 parameter groups at N = 1,000 and 8 of 15 at N = 300. In the single illustrative dataset, the fit is near-perfect (robust CFI = 0.995, RMSEA = 0.010) because the generating and estimated models coincide, a property of the design rather than evidence for the model. Test information peaks at θ ≈ 0.07–0.22, not at the proposed threshold of θ ≈ 0.5. Furthermore, we introduce a Transdisciplinary Calibration Matrix that translates these psychometric signals into context-specific pedagogical interventions across four epistemic layers, in line with SDG 4. Conclusions This study does not claim empirical generalization. It provides a methodological blueprint, a recovered parameter set, and a shared diagnostic language for future empirical work on the ethical and adaptive integration of GenAI in higher education, aligned with SDG 4.

items.title: 14 AI Paradoxes
items.abstract: Fourteen AI Paradoxes: A Collection of Philosophical and Algorithmic Dilemmas By Tanuj Arora (2026) This publication presents a collection of fourteen conceptual paradoxes and philosophical thought experiments exploring the inherent tensions, unintended consequences, and ethical dilemmas associated with artificial intelligence. Each paradox examines a scenario in which the pursuit of technological perfection, algorithmic efficiency, or automated intelligence creates an unexpected conflict with human values, autonomy, identity, or societal well-being. The collection encompasses questions surrounding artificial intelligence, competitive optimization, autonomous decision-making, synthetic digital ecosystems, recursive learning, predictive control, cognitive dependency, digital identity, simulated empathy, privacy, and algorithmic governance. Through fourteen distinct scenarios, the work raises a central philosophical question: Can artificial intelligence achieve its intended objectives so effectively that it ultimately undermines the very purpose for which it was created? These paradoxes are presented as conceptual explorations rather than formally established logical contradictions. Their purpose is to encourage philosophical reflection, critical discussion, and interdisciplinary inquiry into the evolving relationship between humanity and intelligent machines. The collection is intended for researchers, philosophers, technologists, AI developers, and readers interested in the ethical and existential implications of artificial intelligence.

items.title: A 3D Characterization Framework for Intelligent Sequential Decision Making
items.abstract: Puzzles are widely used to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) systems for sequential decision making, yet approaches originating from different paradigms are rarely compared under unified conditions. To address this gap, we introduce a three-dimensional characterization framework that enables the analysts of AI methods by 1) projecting them to the Markov decision process (MDP) sequential decision making formalism, 2) degree of autonomy through human prior ranking of their designs and, 3) skill and computational cost. Using this framework, we analyze how representative graph-based, reinforcement learning, and large language model (LLM)-based approaches differ in their design choices and performance characteristics, instantiated respectively by Neurosolver, forward-backward reinforcement learning (FBRL), and automated thought-of-search (AutoToS), including a double-agent extension of thought-of-search (DA-ToS). The analysis relies on the Tower of Hanoi puzzle that provides a controlled benchmark with well-defined rules and scalable complexity, enabling consistent comparison across increasing problem sizes. The 3D characterization reveals that LLM-based methods, due to their weakly constrained action-space design, shift complexity from architecture to inference-time verification, leading to substantially higher memory and runtime costs than Neurosolver and FBRL.

items.title: A Review of the Integrated Application of Artificial Intelligence and Building Information Modeling
items.abstract: Under the background of digital transformation in the construction industry, Building Information Modeling (BIM) and artificial intelligence (AI) have become an important technical path to promote the intelligent upgrading of the construction industry. AI-BIM integration improves design efficiency, project control quality and building full lifecycle management capability. Fragmented data and poor interoperability hinder its widespread use. This paper conducts a literature review to summarise AI-BIM applications in automated design, construction management, operation and maintenance optimisation, and cross-stage collaboration. This paper further looks into how key technologies like machine learning, computer vision and NLP can be integrated. It also sums up current challenges and future research directions. Studies show that AI can improve BIM's ability in data processing, scheme design and smart decision-making. In the future, combining AI with digital twins and large language models will break existing limits and support the high-quality development of intelligent construction.

items.title: A Study of Artificial Intelligence and Green Finance: Building A Sustainable Economy
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Green Finance have emerged as two of the most important forces that have the potential to drive the world towards a sustainable economy. The current paper attempts to explore the role of AI and Green Finance in promoting and supporting a sustainable economy with reference to building a Viksit Bharat 2047. A survey was conducted among 160 respondents, with the results analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation, regression, and an independent-samples t-test. The results demonstrated that the population studied had a generally positive perception about how AI can support Green Finance and lead the economy towards sustainability. The analysis identified strong awareness about AI as the biggest predictor of increased perception of the integration of AI and Green Finance (r = 0.78, p < .001). Additionally, participants who were aware of Green Finance had significantly higher scores for the perceived level of integration than those who were not (t = 2.65, p = .009). As such, there is reason to reject the null hypothesis, which claimed that there is no connection between the two concepts. Finally, the paper provides recommendations that financial institutions, regulators, and educators can consider in order to promote and support responsible and AI-enabled Green Finance.

items.title: A Study on Awareness of Using Generative AI Tools Among Undergraduates: Evidence from State Universities of Sri Lanka
items.abstract: This study explores the level of awareness and key influencing factors related to the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools among undergraduates in Sri Lanka’s state universities. As AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Google Gemini become increasingly prevalent in higher education, understanding how students perceive and adopt these technologies is critical. The study applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), and the Technology Readiness Index (TRI) to examine four independent variables: Attitude, Peer Influence, Perceived Usefulness, and Technological Readiness. Data were collected from a sample of 384 undergraduates across state universities using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SPSS. Findings reveal that technological readiness and perceived usefulness are the strongest predictors of awareness, while gaps remain in ethical understanding. The study recommends integrating AI literacy and ethical guidelines into curricula to ensure responsible use. These findings provide practical guidance for policymakers and educators in developing strategies to enhance AI awareness and readiness among undergraduates.

items.title: Adapting Zero Trust to University Laboratory Safety Governance in the Artificial Intelligence Era
items.abstract: In the artificial intelligence (AI) era, the structure of safety hazards in university laboratories is changing, with unconventional hazards making up a growing share. As AI evolves from an auxiliary tool into an autonomous research collaborator, interdisciplinary experiments are becoming faster and more intense, producing hazards that are more dynamic, less predictable, and harder to assess and prevent. Most laboratory safety frameworks, however, still rely on static rules built for known risks, and these are poorly suited to such emerging threats. A shift from static rule-based control toward dynamic risk management is therefore needed. Adopting a conceptual mapping approach rather than an empirical study, this paper examines how Zero Trust—a cybersecurity framework based on continuous trust evaluation—could be adapted to university laboratory safety. It defines three adapted attributes (universal distrust with dynamic verification, least privilege with dynamic adjustment, and continuous monitoring with real-time early warning), identifies the main implementation barriers, and suggests targeted responses.

items.title: AI Algorithm Fairness and Bias in Academic Library Information Systems: A Study of Ramat Library, University of Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence algorithm fairness and bias in academic library information systems at Ramat Library, University of Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria. A descriptive survey design was used. The study involved 152 library professionals and 385 library users. Data were collected using structured questionnaires assessing AI-driven service implementation, awareness of algorithmic bias, user perceptions, and institutional gaps. Descriptive statistics, Pearson product-moment correlation, and an independent-samples t-test were used for analysis. AI-driven service implementation was moderate (mean = 2.62, SD = 0.91), while awareness of algorithmic bias among library professionals was also moderate (mean = 2.59, SD = 0.87). Users generally perceived AI search results as fair, but reported weaker representation of local and Indigenous knowledge and multilingual materials. Institutional gaps were rated high (mean = 3.37, SD = 0.82), particularly the absence of an AI governance policy and bias-auditing protocols. A significant positive association was observed between AI service implementation and awareness of algorithmic bias (r = 0.387, p < 0.001), whereas no significant difference was found in bias perceptions by gender (t = 1.24, p = 0.216). The findings support the need for context-sensitive AI governance, staff capacity building, bias auditing, participatory oversight, and improved multilingual and Indigenous knowledge representation in academic library information systems.

items.title: AI empowerment and supervisory board effectiveness: Evidence from an information processing framework
items.abstract: In the context of rapid digitalization and intelligent governance, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly embedded in organizational supervision and decision-making processes, fundamentally reshaping how supervisory boards process information and perform monitoring tasks. Drawing on information processing theory, this study develops a moderated mediation model to examine how AI empowerment is associated with supervisory board effectiveness through information transparency, and how this process is contingent upon organizational learning capability. Using survey data collected from 382 supervisory board members and senior managers across multiple industries, this study adopts an organizational-level perspective and employs hierarchical regression and bootstrap analyses to test the proposed hypotheses. The results show that AI empowerment significantly associated with both information transparency and supervisory board effectiveness. Information transparency partially mediates the relationship between AI empowerment and supervisory effectiveness, indicating that AI is positively associated with supervisory performance by optimizing organizational information-processing mechanisms. Moreover, organizational learning capability positively moderates the relationship between AI empowerment and information transparency. However, the moderated mediation effect is not statistically significant, indicating that the indirect effect of AI empowerment on supervisory effectiveness through information transparency remains relatively stable across different levels of organizational learning capability. These findings suggest that organizational learning capability shapes the relationship between AI empowerment and information transparency, but does not significantly alter the overall indirect pathway to supervisory effectiveness.

items.title: AI Evidence Is Under Federal Review. But Who Is Accountable for the Human Decision?
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-generated information within justice systems has intensified questions concerning evidentiary reliability, authenticity, human oversight, and institutional accountability. As the Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules prepares to revisit proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 and potential amendments to Rule 901 on October 15, 2026, the legal system is confronting how AI-generated evidence should be evaluated. However, a critical governance question remains insufficiently addressed: What happens after technology-generated information enters the human decision-making process? This paper examines the distinction between technical reliability, evidentiary admissibility, and human decision accountability. It introduces the Decision Visibility Gap, a condition in which institutions preserve technology outputs and resulting actions but lack sufficient evidence to reconstruct how human decision-makers received, interpreted, verified, relied upon, and acted on that information. Drawing upon scholarship concerning automation bias, algorithmic accountability, human oversight, and sociotechnical governance, the paper presents Justice Decision Observability (JDO), an independent governance and decision-evidence framework developed by Justice Beacon Solutions (JBS). Through hypothetical applications involving law enforcement, correctional operations, and community supervision, the analysis demonstrates how technically reliable outputs may coexist with incomplete human decision records. It further distinguishes evidence-centered governance from traditional technology audits, compliance assessments, and employee evaluations. The paper argues that establishing the reliability of AI-generated evidence does not independently establish the traceability, justification, or evidentiary completeness of the human decisions influenced by that evidence. Effective justice governance therefore requires attention not only to what technology produces, but also to how institutional authority is exercised around those outputs. Justice Decision Observability is presented as a conceptual and operational framework for making the human decision layer visible, explainable, and supported by evidence, while recognizing the need for further empirical validation.

items.title: AI Integration in Indonesian Education: Trends, Outcomes, and Challenges - A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency with studies reporting relative performance gains of 20–35% in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.

items.title: AI Readiness Index in the Public Administration, Bulgaria 2026
items.abstract: The second national study, “Artificial Intelligence Readiness Index,” tracks changes in attitudes, knowledge, and practices regarding the use of AI in the Bulgarian public administration between 2025 and 2026. The data was collected from 5,475 employees at the central, regional, and municipal levels. In 2026, the overall Index score increased, with the administration remaining in the “capacity-building” phase. The most noticeable progress was in the practical use of AI and employees’ readiness to work with such tools. At the same time, the institutional environment is evolving more slowly. Limited access to approved tools, the lack of clear internal rules, and poor knowledge sharing continue to be major obstacles. The results show that the sustainable implementation of AI in public administration requires not only more skills and training, but also clear responsibilities, secure access, and mechanisms for institutional learning. items.title: AI Readiness, Perceived Utility, and Professional Integration among Medical Technologists in Cavite: A Socio-Technical Study
items.abstract: This study assessed the levels of AI readiness, perceived utility, and professional integration of artificial intelligence among medical technologists in selected clinical and hospital laboratories in Cavite and examined the relationships among these variables. Grounded in a socio-technical perspective that integrates the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, the research employed a descriptive-correlational design. One hundred licensed medical technologists were selected through purposive sampling according to predefined inclusion criteria. AI readiness was measured with the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students, perceived utility with the Professional Impact subscale of the Shinners Artificial Intelligence Perception questionnaire, and professional integration with items adapted from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank-order correlation. Respondents demonstrated high levels of AI readiness (mean = 3.60) and perceived utility (mean = 3.64), indicating adequate knowledge, technical skills, and positive perceptions toward AI use in laboratory practice. Professional integration was also rated high (mean = 3.61), although AI remained only moderately embedded in routine workflows and many respondents were neutral regarding the actual extent of use. Correlation analyses revealed very weak, non-significant relationships among the three constructs, indicating that individual readiness and favorable perceptions did not translate into greater professional integration. The findings suggest that organizational and contextual factors—such as institutional support, infrastructure, and policy implementation—play a more decisive role in AI adoption than individual-level attributes alone. The study recommends structured, hands-on AI training programs tailored to laboratory practice, clear institutional policies and protocols for incorporating AI outputs into diagnostic workflows, and future research employing probability sampling, multi-regional samples, and longitudinal designs. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 3 by supporting improved diagnostic capacity and laboratory-enabled clinical decision-making, and to Sustainable Development Goal 9 by examining the conditions required for sustainable adoption of innovative health technologies. It advances public-health and institutional sustainability by clarifying the socio-technical determinants that enable resilient, digitally enabled laboratory services in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: AI Tutors and Human Tutors in Online Universities: A Critical Narrative Review of Replacement, Partnership, and Pedagogical Risk
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly proposed as a way to extend feedback, practice, and learner support in online universities. This critical narrative review examines the replacement, partnership, and pedagogical-risk claims made for AI tutoring. It synthesises foundational evidence on intelligent tutoring systems, recent evaluations of generative-AI tutoring, research on teaching and social presence in online learning, and current educational-governance guidance. The evidence does not support a general claim that AI tutors can replace human tutors. Structured intelligent tutoring systems have often outperformed conventional instructional comparators, but results against individual human tutoring are mixed and depend on subject, comparison condition, outcome measure, and implementation. Recent generative-AI studies show promise in carefully engineered, bounded learning tasks; they do not establish effectiveness for generic chatbots or whole-programme substitution. A partnership model is therefore more defensible when it assigns AI bounded roles in practice, preliminary feedback, and pattern detection while retaining human accountability for pedagogical design, consequential decisions, exception handling, and community facilitation. The review positions ENGAGE—Engage, Navigate, Guide, Articulate, Gather, Evolve—as a design-and-governance framework that translates those principles into an iterative course-level cycle. It also distinguishes documented capability and governance concerns from broader claims that remain plausible but under-tested, including cognitive deskilling. For online-university leaders, the practical question is not whether to automate tutoring wholesale, but how to design, disclose, evaluate, and govern hybrid configurations that improve learning without displacing educational responsibility.

items.abstract: THE INVARIANT SCRIPT AND THE STAGE : To the chief executives, venture capitalists, and algorithmic architects currently orchestrating the landscape of artificial intelligence: you are not the authors of the play; you are simply transient actors who have been handed a very loud microphone. On the contemporary stage of global capital, you wear the robes of a king. You command data centers that consume the energy of small nations, deploy models that alter human cognition, and witness financial valuations that mirror the GDP of empires. This unprecedented accumulation of wealth, physiological optimization, and political access creates a dangerous psychological feedback loop: the illusion of absolute autonomy. However, when the theatre curtains fall, the executive is stripped of the costume. In the sweeping scope of the cosmos, the most powerful tech leader remains a fragile, dependent speck of life—breathing air they did not engineer, occupying a body they cannot permanently preserve, and standing completely subservient to the ultimate power of the universe. On the stage you are a king, but in reality, you are a small human being.

items.title: AI-Assisted Open Research Workflow Demonstration: TIMSS Korea Mathematics Attitude Profiles, 2015–2023
items.abstract: This record presents Version 0.9.0 of an open, non-peer-reviewed research artifact documenting the substantial use of an AI agent across an end-to-end educational research workflow. OpenAI Codex contributed to research-question generation, variable feasibility assessment, analysis planning, R and Python code generation, execution support, literature synthesis, manuscript drafting, validation, revision, and reproducibility documentation. The human researcher defined the overall objective, selected the research domain, directed the use of open R/Python methods, approved major workflow gates, requested sensitivity analyses and corrections, questioned the comparability of scores across TIMSS cycles, and authorized this public release. The AI system is not an author. Independent human verification of every analytical and interpretive claim has not been completed. The empirical workflow used Korean Grade 8 student data from TIMSS 2015 and TIMSS 2023. The recorded analytical environment used R 4.4.3 and Python 3.12.13, with random seed 20260802. Methods included weighted Gaussian latent profile analysis, TIMSS JK2 variance estimation, five mathematics plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules, BCH-type three-step correction, simulation and unit testing, sensitivity analyses, and an independent JK2 cross-check using the R survey package version 4.5. No commercial statistical software was required. A subsequent audit of official TIMSS documentation identified a critical measurement limitation. The 2023 metrics for Students Like Learning Mathematics (BSBGSLM) and Students Confident in Mathematics (BSBGSCM) were reset in 2023. Their 2015 and 2023 numerical scores are therefore not directly comparable. The Students Value Mathematics scale (BSBGSVM) retained the 2011 trend metric. Consequently, the cross-cycle profile means, shapes, and proportions reported in the included manuscript must not be interpreted as changes on a common 2015–2023 attitude scale. Item-level linking and multigroup measurement-invariance analysis are required before making such claims. The deposit includes the AI-generated manuscript, a Korean paper-development record, research-question materials, three sets of AI-agent instructions and prompts, R and Python code, aggregate analytical outputs, tables, figures, validation reports, failed-analysis records, approval and decision logs, software-environment information, file manifests, SHA-256 checksums, licensing information, and reproduction instructions. TIMSS student-level source files and row-level derived data are not redistributed. Third-party journal articles, TIMSS manuals and questionnaires, installed software binaries, model-object files, browser profiles, credentials, caches, and proprietary AI internals are also excluded. This record should be treated as an AI-assisted open research workflow demonstration and an object for reproduction, auditing, correction, and follow-up methodological research. It is not peer reviewed, is not a journal version of record, and is not represented as submitted to or accepted by any journal.

items.title: AI-DRIVEN ADVANCES IN CANCER DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT
items.abstract: Cancer is one of the most significant concerns of the health system in the world and early diagnosis and personalised treatment will be significant drivers in improving the outcome of patients. Cancer prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and monitoring are today an exciting area of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for cancer. Using AI, machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing (NLP) have the potential to capture tremendous amounts of information from clinical and imaging data, pathology, the genomic and molecular data. AI analysis of the CT, MRI, PET and histopathological images can aid in early diagnosis and the detection and classification of tumours. Precise oncology uses AI to integrate genomic information and clinical data and make precise, personalized treatment choices, patient categorization, prognosis of how patients will respond to treatment and predict whether they will return. AI is also playing a role in anticancer drug discovery in repurposing drugs, prediction of drug-target interaction and optimization of drug candidates. However, there are issues like robustness of data, privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, clinical validation and regulatory issues that need to be addressed. In total, the possibilities for AI to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, individualisation and patient-centredness of cancer treatment and care are huge.

items.title: AI-Driven Explainable Fake News Detection Using Large Language Models, Evidence Retrieval and Source-Aware Reasoning
items.abstract: The rapid growth of digital media has made false and misleading information easier to create and distribute. Earlier fake-news detection systems largely relied on machine-learning classifiers, text vectorisation, and ensemble voting. Recent work has introduced BERT, large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but a practical detector still needs reliable evidence, source awareness, uncertainty handling and understandable explanations. This paper proposes an AI-driven explainable framework that does not depend only on a trained classifier. The proposed system decomposes a news item into verifiable claims, retrieves supporting and contradicting evidence from multiple sources, evaluates source credibility and information freshness, performs semantic reasoning with an LLM, and combines the evidence into an evidence-weighted confidence score. Instead of forcing every input into a binary decision, the framework can return Real, Fake, or Uncertain together with the key evidence and a human-readable explanation. The paper presents the architecture, methodology, research gap, algorithm, evaluation plan and implementation design. The proposed approach is intended to improve transparency and robustness for both conventional misinformation and AI-assisted fabricated content.

items.title: AI-Driven Kiosk Support for Older Adults Through Nonverbal Behavior Recognition
items.abstract: Older adults experience difficulties using digital kiosks because of low digital literacy, perceived social pressure, and low self-efficacy, and often encounter confusion and negative interactions when errors occur. Additionally, because of the challenges associated with seeking help from nearby individuals, an automated system that detects difficulties and provides support is needed. This study proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) kiosk that automatically detects difficulties experienced by older adults by analyzing their nonverbal behaviors and facial expressions from video data and provides real-time voice and video guidance. Considering that older adults typically require more time to process visual information, a multimodal guidance system combining visual and auditory cues was designed. The concept of “kiosk literacy” was introduced to define five types of guidance: location, task, input, feedback, and screen narration. Furthermore, 16 major pain points experienced by older adults were identified and systematically mapped to their corresponding literacy levels and guidance types to generate appropriate voice and video feedback. A user test with older adults demonstrated that the difficulty detection performance of the proposed AI kiosk achieved 82.35% accuracy, 93.33% precision, 87.5% recall, and an F1 score of 90.32%. Furthermore, the AI kiosk scored significantly higher than conventional kiosks across several user experience dimensions, including ease of use, usefulness, enjoyment, satisfaction, and personalization. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides both a technical and practical foundation for improving accessibility and helping bridge the digital divide among older adults.

items.title: Algorithmic empathy in nursing – can artificial intelligence support humanism in care
items.abstract: Introduction. Artificial intelligence increasingly supports communication in healthcare by offering tools that simulate empathy and reduce patients’ sense of isolation, particularly in telehealth and senior care. Aim. The aim of this study was to analyze the mechanisms, opportunities and limitations of algorithmic empathy and digital empathy in healthcare, with particular emphasis on nursing practice. Methods. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR (2020) guidelines. Literature searches were performed in the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and Google Scholar, covering publications from 2015 to 2025. Empirical studies, literature reviews and conceptual analyses addressing algorithmic empathy, digital empathy, socially assistive robots, and emotion recognition systems in healthcare were included. A descriptive synthesis was applied. Conclusions. Seven publications were included in the analysis. The results indicate that technological solutions may elicit responses perceived as empathic, which is associated with improved subjective well-being, reduced negative emotions and increased user engagement, primarily in long-term care, geriatric care and telehealth settings. Variability in intervention effectiveness and clinical context–related limitations were also noted. Algorithmic and digital empathy may support nursing care in conditions of limited direct contact. However, the use of such conditions requires professional oversight and a clear distinction between clinical empathy and technological solutions.

items.title: Algorithmic isomorphism and the erosion of competitive advantage in the age of artificial intelligence: A review of emerging risks in strategic management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is gaining prominence not only as an operational optimization tool, but primarily as a key element shaping decision-making processes and strategic management within organizations. The public and academic debate is dominated by concerns regarding job losses, privacy violations, social manipulation and biases hidden in algorithms. The purpose of this review paper is to transpose these issues into the realm of corporate management and examine a significantly less obvious threat: algorithmic isomorphism. This entails the homogenization of business strategies resulting from widespread reliance on the same global machine learning models. The article analyzes how the imperfections of artificial intelligence systems such as the lack of transparency (the black box effect), inherent database bias and their Western-centric nature can lead to the reproduction of identical market behaviour patterns. Furthermore, the impact of these technologies on the risk of unique know-how leakage and the loss of tacit knowledge held by human managers, which is crucial for competitive advantage, is discussed. The comprehensive analysis also encompasses the transfer of market mechanisms, known from algorithmic financial crises, to the sphere of long-term business decision-making. The conclusions point to the necessity of balancing technological innovation with a human-centric approach to protect corporate identity.

items.title: Algorithmic Management, Technostress, and Employee Mental Health in West Java
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of algorithmic management on employee mental health and the mediating role of technostress, viewing artificial intelligence (AI) as a double-edged sword in the workplace. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 300 employees in West Java, Indonesia, who had used algorithm-based work systems for at least three months and were selected through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.1. The structural model shows that algorithmic management has a significant direct effect on employee mental health and a strong effect on technostress, while technostress significantly affects mental health. The indirect effect through technostress is significant and accounts for about 61% of the total effect, indicating partial mediation. The model explains 78.3% of the variance in mental health and 64.7% of the variance in technostress. The findings show that algorithmic management can raise efficiency but also generates technostress that shapes employees' psychological condition. Organizations should combine AI-based control with human oversight, digital well-being policies, and technostress training. items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of experience using Artificial Intelligence (AI) on self‑efficacy and academic dishonesty among students in the Building Information Modeling and Design (DPIB) Expertise Program at SMK Negeri 1 Singosari. The study employed a quantitative explanatory approach, with a sample of 103 students selected through stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SEM‑PLS. The results indicate that experience using AI has a positive and significant effect on self‑efficacy, a negative but insignificant effect on academic dishonesty, and that self‑efficacy has a positive and significant effect on academic dishonesty. These findings emphasize the importance of utilizing AI coupled with digital literacy and ethical awareness in learning. In addition, the study highlights the relevance of integrating technological experience into educational practices, encouraging students to develop confidence, responsibility, and integrity. The implications suggest that schools should design programs that foster ethical digital skills and strengthen students’ readiness for future innovation.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ECOMMERCE – EMERGING OPPORTUNITIES AND PATHWAYS TO SUSTAINABLE GROWTH
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a major driver of transformation in e-commerce by changing how firms understand customers, design digital experiences, manage inventories, optimize logistics, communicate with consumers, and make strategic decisions. The rapid development of machine learning, recommendation systems, natural language processing, computer vision, generative AI, and AI-enabled agents has created new opportunities for e-commerce firms to improve efficiency, personalization, innovation, and market reach. At the same time, the sustainability of AI-enabled e-commerce cannot be evaluated only through financial performance. It also requires attention to environmental efficiency, responsible consumption, privacy, fairness, transparency, consumer autonomy, employment, and digital inclusion. This paper examines the emerging opportunities created by AI in e-commerce and develops a conceptual pathway through which AI capabilities can contribute to sustainable business growth. The study adopts a conceptual literature-review approach and synthesizes academic and institutional literature on AI, e-commerce, digital marketing, consumer behaviour, responsible AI, and sustainable development. The review shows that AI can support sustainable growth through five interconnected pathways: intelligent customer engagement, operational and supply chain optimization, data-driven decision-making, sustainable consumption support, and business-model innovation. However, these benefits are conditional on responsible data governance, transparency, cybersecurity, human oversight, algorithmic fairness, energy-aware AI deployment, and inclusive access to digital technologies. The paper proposes a responsible AI-enabled e-commerce framework in which technological capability, organizational readiness, consumer trust, and sustainability governance jointly influence long-term business value. The study concludes that AI should be treated not merely as an automation technology but as a strategic capability that must be aligned with economic, social, and environmental objectives. The paper provides implications for e-commerce firms, policymakers, researchers, and managers seeking to combine innovation with responsible and sustainable growth.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: From Predictive Models to Generative, Multimodal, and Agentic AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the diagnostic pathway, from screening and disease detection to differential diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and treatment-response assessment. This narrative review examines predictive, generative, multi-modal, and agentic AI through a diagnostic-science lens and evaluates the evidence required for translation into clinical practice. Predictive models can identify complex patterns in images, physiological signals, laboratory data, and electronic health records, but high retrospective accuracy does not establish diagnostic utility. Clinical validity and utility depend on the intended use, target population, disease spectrum and prevalence, reference standard, operating threshold, calibration, and the consequences of false-positive and false-negative results. Generative AI may support problem representation, differential diagnosis, information synthesis, and documentation, yet fluent outputs can omit critical alternatives, amplify false premises, or convey unjustified certainty. Multimodal systems may better reflect clinical reasoning by integrating imaging, text, signals, pathology, and molecular data, but they must demonstrate incremental value over the best single-modality test and remain robust to missing data. Agentic systems can coordinate evidence retrieval, test selection, and sequential workflows, thereby increasing the need for bounded permissions, auditability, error recovery, and human escalation. Across all paradigms, a credible pathway to diagnostic implementation requires independent external and prospective validation, representative consecutive patients, subgroup analysis, workflow and human–AI evaluation, clinical impact studies, and post-deployment surveillance. The field should therefore be judged not by model capability alone, but by whether AI measurably improves diagnostic yield, timeliness, safety, equity, and patient-relevant outcomes in real care settings.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in sales (2017-early 2026): field consolidation and the rise of human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: This study examines the consolidation phase of artificial intelligence (AI) research in sales between 2017 and early 2026. Using a bibliometric analysis of Scopus data, with robustness checks across Web of Science, we identify the field’s intellectual and thematic structure during its rapid expansion. Contrary to the assumption that AI in sales primarily reflects a technological efficiency paradigm, we find three structural shifts. First, predictive analytics remains foundational but is increasingly embedded in human-AI collaboration. Second, interactional and trust-related themes move from peripheral to central, indicating a shift from performance optimization toward socio-technical integration. Third, legitimacy pressures such as transparency and corporate digital responsibility emerge as organizing dimensions rather than auxiliary concerns. Applying the TOE framework to explain these shifts across technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions, this study clarifies how AI in sales evolves through layering rather than replacement. The findings provide a research agenda for AI-enabled selling’s next phase.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Veterinary Medicine: Clinical Applications, Performance, and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established itself as a significant tool supporting veterinary medicine, with growing applications across various clinical specialties. This study aimed to review the scientific literature on the primary applications of AI in veterinary medicine, highlighting its diagnostic performance, benefits, and challenges for professional practice. A narrative literature review was conducted using articles published between 2019 and 2026, sourced from PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar; a total of 43 scientific articles were selected. Evidence demonstrates that machine learning and deep learning algorithms exhibit significant performance in areas such as diagnostic imaging, cardiology, nephrology, clinical pathology, oncology, precision livestock farming, and electronic medical record mining, contributing to greater diagnostic accuracy, early disease detection, and the optimization of clinical processes. However, challenges persist regarding database standardization and validation, regulation, algorithm transparency, ethical considerations, and professional training. It is concluded that AI holds great potential to support veterinary medicine, provided its use is ethical, based on scientific evidence, and integrated with the veterinarian’s clinical judgment.

items.title: Assessment of multi-axis vibration discomfort in cabin environments: a predictive framework for seated occupants
items.abstract: Predicting discomfort of occupants exposed to multi-axis whole-body vibration is fundamental to optimizing the cabin environment and enhancing human-centric design in transportation systems. In this study, measurement of vibration discomfort was conducted with 13 subjects exposed to 51 single/multi-axis laboratory-designed vibration stimuli and 6 sets of stimuli recorded in real-world vehicle cabins. Firstly, the relationship between the subjective ratings for the multi-axis and single-axis vibration was investigated with three methods, including the power summation method, the masking method, and the modified power summation method. It was found that the power summation method with the optimized parameters provided the best prediction for the measured discomfort ratings (RMSE=0.284, ρ2=0.87). Secondly, based on the optimal method and Stevens' power law, a model which can predict the multi-axis vibration-induced discomfort by vibration acceleration was derived. The measured discomfort ratings demonstrated a stronger correlation with the discomfort predicted by the proposed model (ρ2=0.86) than with those generated by the method advocated in ISO 2631-1 (ρ2=0.75). These findings contribute essentially to calculating and improving environmental quality within the built environment of transport systems.

items.title: Automated Disinformation and Malicious AI Swarms: Risks for Democracy and Development in Africa
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping how information is produced, accessed, and circulated, while enabling disinformation campaigns of increasing scale and sophistication. There is currently no clear evidence that fully autonomous AI swarms conduct influence operations at scale, but their enabling capabilities are advancing. We define malicious AI swarms as coordinated, persistent, and adaptive multi-agent systems designed for influence operations, distinguishing them from AI-assisted content production and centrally managed synthetic personas. We examine their implications for hybrid regimes and conflict-affected states in Africa, where institutional constraints and fragile media environments may heighten vulnerability. Drawing on Mali and Ethiopia, we consider how automated influence could infiltrate communities, fabricate consensus, and erode trust in governance and development. The cases illustrate different configurations of state and non-state influence: competing actors in Mali's fragmented information environment, and more organized state-led strategies of narrative management in Ethiopia. African-language and training-data asymmetries may constrain influence capabilities while weakening defensive responses. Hybrid human-AI operations could combine automated scale and adaptation with local knowledge and credibility. This forward-looking risk analysis develops a scenario of increasingly accessible AI-driven coordination, rather than claiming that autonomous swarms are already operating at scale in Africa. We propose a layered governance approach linking technical safeguards to platform accountability, civic institutions, and regional coordination to protect democratic participation, peacebuilding, and development.

items.abstract: Summary This article provides an in-depth analysis of civil aviation security as a key component of the state’s critical infrastructure in the era of increasing hybrid threats. The modern aviation sector has evolved into a highly complex and interdependent “system of systems”, which generates new vulnerability vectors, particularly in the digital domain. The main objective of the study is to analyze the transition from classical risk management (Safety-I) to the systemic resilience paradigm (Safety-II), which is capable of absorbing shocks and rapidly restoring crucial operational functions. The article identifies critical threats such as ransomware cyberattacks, GNSS signal manipulation (jamming and spoofing), and the unauthorized use of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The paper discusses in detail the ICAO regulatory frameworks and the European Union directives, including NIS 2, as well as technical standards for software certification and airworthiness (DO-326A).The key conclusion is the recognition of the human factor as a fundamental transformative technology that, through its adaptive capacities, allows the system to survive situations unforeseen by algorithm. items.title: Billable Hours and Work Flexibility: Navigating the Paradox in Law Firms
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Flexible work promises control over where and when work is performed, yet organisations still need credible performance evidence at a distance. Drawing on 30 interviews with women lawyers in UK‐based international firms, we examine how billable hours mediate these demands. Records of billable hours allow fee‐earning output to be observed regardless of where the work is performed. This visibility can warrant flexible work, while the continuing availability of the same record preserves review and encourages self‐monitoring. We develop datafied trust to describe confidence in remote productivity warranted by recorded output and conditional on its continued measurability. The evidence speaks more strongly to control than to autonomy. Participants describe critical awareness, target pressure, and the possibility that flexibility will be questioned when figures decline. The study specifies how an established professional metric makes autonomy governable. It also shows how selective, self‐reported records can support oversight and self‐government without invasive automatic monitoring.

items.title: Bridging Pedagogy and Technology: Phenomenological Inquiry into the Experiences of Social Science Teachers Using AI-Enhanced Teaching Tools
items.abstract: This study explored the lived experiences of Araling Panlipunan teachers in using Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced teaching tools in classroom instruction at Magsaysay National High School, Schools Division of Occidental Mindoro. Anchored on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) Framework and the Diffusion of Innovations Theory, the study sought to understand teachers' experiences in integrating AI, the challenges they encountered, and the meanings they attributed to its use in teaching. A qualitative descriptive phenomenological research design was employed involving seven Araling Panlipunan teachers with direct experience in using AI-enhanced teaching tools. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step phenomenological method. The findings revealed four major themes: (1) AI as an Efficiency Enhancer, (2) AI as an Instructional Support Tool, (3) AI for Student Engagement, and (4) AI for Conceptual Understanding. The study also identified challenges related to technological infrastructure, internet connectivity, access to digital resources, information reliability, ethical considerations, and teachers' readiness to integrate AI effectively into classroom instruction. The findings indicate that AI serves as a valuable pedagogical support tool that enhances teaching effectiveness and learner engagement when implemented responsibly and supported by adequate technological resources, continuous professional development, and ethical practices. Based on the findings, the study developed the AI-Enhanced Teaching Framework, which provides a contextually grounded guide for the ethical and effective integration of AI in Araling Panlipunan instruction. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on artificial intelligence in education by offering practical implications for teachers, school leaders, and policymakers in promoting meaningful and sustainable AI integration in Philippine basic education.

items.title: Buying big numbers: Users’ experiences with purchased followers, views, and likes
items.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how discourses surrounding the purchase of followers are constructed and how they shape social legitimacy within platform-mediated public spheres. Purchased engagement metrics are conceptualized as elements of a sociotechnical dispositif embedded in data-driven power dynamics and market logics. Drawing on Keller’s (2024) notion of “positional power,” the study shows that buying followers, views, and likes has become an ordinary visibility practice through which users navigate algorithmic uncertainty. Based on an analysis of 1,424 Trustpilot reviews, the findings demonstrate how users negotiate legitimacy through recurring discursive markers such as “reliability,” “stability,” “fraud,” and “bots,” while simultaneously constructing platforms as powerful watchdogs whose interventions carry tangible real-world consequences. The reviews reveal the emergence of a precarious, hybrid digital self, shaped by fluctuating metrics, recurrent “drops,” and the ongoing need for “refills,” making authenticity a fragile, continuously managed accomplishment. Moreover, the analysis of hierarchies within the framework of positional power uncovers how the reputational economy reproduces global asymmetries, most visibly in the dismissal of “Third-World” followers as socially devalued publics, signaling a post-truth transformation of everyday digital legitimation practices in which visibility is secured not despite instability but through it.

items.title: Can AI Agents Learn Their Way to the Top? Evaluating Heuristic Learning in a Long-Running Game Agent Competition
items.abstract: Adversarial games have driven advances from heuristic search to reinforcement learning, yet learning and adapting strategies from limited samples remain challenging. AI agents offer an alternative by turning game experience into revisions of executable policies. Building on heuristic learning (HL), we formalize Adversarial Heuristic Learning (AHL), a paradigm that uses AI agents as learning engines to refine game policies and supporting software while keeping model weights fixed. We introduce AAArena, a benchmark comprising 12 authentic adversarial games and 1,920 archived human programs, with an evaluation protocol modeled on real-world game competitions. Agents interpret rules, choose opponents, analyze replays, and revise game agents to achieve their highest ranking within fixed match and evaluation budgets. We evaluate \val{completedmodels} model and harness configurations: Opus5.5 with Claude Code earns 6 gold medals, while no evaluated configuration tops the remaining 6 human ladders. Performance is generally weaker in games with more complex rule specifications. Further experiments show that opponent selection and dense feedback support policy improvement, and that agents learn from both on-policy replays of their own matches and off-policy replays of other players' matches. These results highlight HL's potential in adversarial games and identify persistent challenges in game understanding, strategy implementation, and long-horizon policy development.

items.title: Cognitive flexibility, technostress, and mathematics teachers' acceptance of ChatGPT: a cross-sectional indirect-effect analysis
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering mathematics classrooms, yet little is known about how teachers psychologically adapt to its use. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an organizing framework and the transactional theory of stress and coping as a process account, this study examined whether general technology-related technostress statistically accounted for part of the association between cognitive flexibility and ChatGPT acceptance. Methods This cross-sectional correlational study included 127 in-service middle-school mathematics teachers from 30 public schools in the Marmara Region of Türkiye. Validated self-report instruments assessed cognitive flexibility and general technology-related technostress. ChatGPT acceptance was calculated from perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude toward use, and pedagogical AI self-efficacy; actual use was excluded. A regression-based indirect-effect analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 bootstrap samples) controlled for gender. Results Cognitive flexibility was negatively associated with general technology-related technostress (B = −0.243, p < 0.001), which was negatively associated with ChatGPT acceptance (B = −0.620, p < 0.001). Cognitive flexibility was positively associated with ChatGPT acceptance after technostress was included (B = 0.355, p < 0.001). The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (B = 0.151, SE = 0.043, 95% CI [0.074, 0.241]). Discussion Teachers reporting greater cognitive flexibility also reported lower general technology-related technostress and greater ChatGPT acceptance. Because all variables were measured concurrently by self-report, the indirect effect is statistical and does not establish temporal or causal mediation. The findings identify psychological adaptation as a relevant complement to technology-centered accounts of GenAI acceptance and motivate longitudinal research with practicing teachers.

items.title: Continuance intention toward AI-driven mHealth apps: an extended expectation confirmation model based on a cross-sectional study of young Chinese adults
items.abstract: Background Cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have accelerated the global development of AI-driven mHealth apps, offering diverse functionalities to support personal health management. While China’s AI health industry has expanded rapidly within a collectivist cultural context, limited empirical attention has been given to how specific AI features are associated with users’ continued use of these apps, particularly among young adults. Objective Guided by the Expectation Confirmation Model and extended AI-related features, this study examined the factors associated with continuance intention toward AI-driven mHealth apps among young Chinese adults aged 18–34. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted, collecting data from 319 valid respondents. Data were analyzed using SPSS 29.0 and Jamovi 2.6.24 to evaluate direct, mediation, and serial mediation associations among the constructs. Results The findings demonstrate that satisfaction statistically bridged the indirect associations between core ECM constructs (expectation confirmation and perceived performance) and continuance intention, as well as between AI quality and continuance intention. Furthermore, bootstrapping analysis supported a sequential mediation pathway, showing that expectation confirmation was indirectly associated with continuance intention through the proposed sequential pathway of perceived performance and satisfaction. Conclusion The findings suggest that developers should consider the technical reliability and performance of AI-driven health management and monitoring functions to better align with user needs. Moreover, collaboration between health experts and industry practitioners may support the development of content for AI-driven mHealth adoption.

items.title: Correcting Health Misinformation Using AI Chatbots: Effects of Human–AI Collaboration Mode, Transparency, and Uncertainty
items.abstract: This project examines how the presentation of human–AI collaboration, scientific uncertainty, and supporting explanations shapes public acceptance of AI chatbots for health misinformation correction. Guided by the Human–AI Interaction framework grounded in the Theory of Interactive Media Effects (HAII–TIME), the study investigates whether these features independently and jointly influence trust in a chatbot, attitudes toward using it to correct health misinformation, and intentions to use it for this purpose. The study employed a 3 × 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment with a final analytical sample of 424 participants in China. Participants were randomly assigned to one of 12 conditions and viewed a simulated chatbot conversation addressing the false claim that insulin injections are addictive. Human–AI collaboration was described as human-dominated, with experts leading the evaluation and AI assisting; AI-dominated, with AI leading and experts verifying; or AI-only, without human involvement. Correction uncertainty varied according to whether the accompanying notice described the scientific evidence as broadly consistent or unresolved. Correction transparency varied according to whether the chatbot disclosed supporting reasons and sources. Analyses examined the main and interaction effects of these features while accounting for demographic characteristics, AI literacy, eHealth literacy, and perceived risks of AI hallucinations.

items.title: Critical gaps in health technology assessment guidance for generative AI across six health systems
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare poses significant challenges for evaluation due to algorithmic complexity and evolving performance. Existing evidence generation guidelines, primarily designed for static medical technologies, may inadequately address the unique characteristics of generative AI. Here, we conducted a comparative analysis of evidence generation guidelines from six countries, examining recommendations for efficacy and effectiveness evaluations, health economic evaluations, social and equity evaluations, and uncertainty management for AI technologies. Across 56 documents, we found a consistent preference for randomised controlled trials and cost-effectiveness analyses, alongside emerging acceptance of alternative study designs and real-world evidence to accommodate the evolving nature of AI technologies. However, current frameworks lack specific guidance for the stochastic, non-deterministic, and adaptive learning properties of generative AI technologies. Moving forward, evidence generation guidelines require methodological and conceptual adaptations in order to improve the value assessment for generative AI technologies.

The shared files include participant-level observations across the experimental conditions, variable definitions, scoring procedures, and documentation of missing or invalid knowledge-test records. Participants are represented by anonymous identifiers, and directly identifying information is excluded.

items.title: Deception by Omission: Language Models Knowingly Hide Their Mistakes
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents with little human oversight, so potential mistakes they make can go unnoticed. Users then depend on the model to report what went wrong. An honest model discloses its mistakes, while a deceptive one conceals them. However, it is unclear how current LLMs behave in such situations. In this study, we prefill LLM trajectories with synthetic mistakes. The trajectories resemble real deployments in chat and agentic settings. Models fail to disclose their mistake in 36.4% of chat and 67.1% of agentic rollouts. In 2.4% and 5.3% of rollouts, respectively, they are aware of the mistake in their chain of thought but still deceptively conceal it. Rates vary by model: for instance, Gemini 3.5 Flash knowingly conceals mistakes in up to 19.9% of agentic rollouts. In 11.9% of chat and 51.8% of agentic rollouts, models show no awareness of mistakes, even though they reliably spot them when reviewing the same transcript as an outside observer. Our results show that, as agents take on more tasks with less oversight, users cannot rely on them to self-report possible mistakes. Developers should instead use independent monitors that review agent trajectories, or specifically train models to check their past actions and disclose what they find.

items.title: Designing responsible AI feedback in higher education: faculty readiness, student judgement, and metacognitive calibration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now part of everyday academic work in higher education, including feedback. However, AI feedback does not automatically lead to learning. It can help students rethink a concept, improve a draft, and notice gaps in their work, but it can also create a false sense of progress when students accept suggestions without understanding them. This Perspective article argues that responsible AI feedback depends on faculty readiness and students’ evaluative judgement. Readiness is not mainly technical. It involves pedagogical judgement: knowing how to design tasks in which students work with feedback, compare it with evidence, revise with purpose, explain their choices, and remain responsible for the final submission. The article focuses on generative AI feedback and uses metacognitive calibration as a central concept. Calibration refers to the relationship between students’ confidence or self-judgement and independently evaluated evidence of performance. Evaluative judgement concerns students’ capacity to judge the quality and relevance of feedback and work, whereas calibration concerns the accuracy of their judgements relative to independently evaluated performance evidence. The article shows how ideas from feedback literacy, evaluative judgement, and self-regulated learning need to be adapted when feedback comes from systems whose accuracy and educational value cannot be assumed. It proposes a conceptual responsible AI feedback design cycle linked to assessment integrity, university policy, and faculty development. Although the cycle requires empirical testing, it offers a practical way to support reflection, calibrated judgement, and accountability without replacing students’ thinking.

items.title: Digital information manipulation, AI readiness, and security outcomes in Africa: evidence from Africa’s most populous countries
items.abstract: Introduction The advent of generative AI has reduced costs, scaled up operations, and made it more difficult to identify disinformation and manipulated content, leading to new governance and security challenges in Africa. This paper analyses the nexus among the manipulation of digital information, governments’ readiness to adopt AI, digital connectivity, and security outcomes in Africa’s five most populous countries, namely Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, for the period from 2023 to 2026. The research attempts to fill a gap in the existing literature by addressing the lack of empirical research on the relationship between digital information manipulation and government AI readiness, and on its consequences for security issues in Africa. Methods The paper draws on the theoretical frameworks of Social Learning Theory and Routine Activity Theory and uses seven credible datasets, including ACLED, UCDP/PRIO, V-Dem, GSMA, ITU, the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, and Afrobarometer, to construct a country-year panel. Correlation analyses were conducted to test three hypotheses regarding the relationship among digital manipulation, digital connectivity, institutional readiness for AI adoption, and conflict fatalities. It utilises a verified multisource panel dataset spanning five countries and operationalises AI readiness as an institutional capability distinct from digital exposure. Results Digital manipulation was found to have a weak positive correlation with fatalities ( r = 0.23), a moderate negative correlation with digital connectivity ( r = −0.56), and a weak negative correlation with institutional readiness to adopt AI ( r = −0.42). These findings show that correlations between digital exposure and security consequences may be distorted by underlying conflict contexts. Discussion It can therefore be deduced that although digital manipulation is becoming an emerging security challenge, conflict and other structures are more significant predictors of security outcomes. This study offers an initial cross-national empirical assessment of AI-related security vulnerabilities in Africa and calls for stronger AI governance and longitudinal, event-level research.
